transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-24
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Sara Gomez (BrightUp Eng Manager), Timothy Lee (BrightUp Platform), Nina Park (BrightUp Security)

Summary:
Quick console walkthrough focused on tracing, error analysis, and request logs for debugging production issues. Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated; security/GDPR and SOC2 scope is critical. Agreed next steps include sending pricing, SOC2/network diagrams, and scheduling a benchmark on Dedicated.

Topics covered:
- Redwood Console tracing overview and how it ties to request logs
- Error analysis workflows and filtering for model/version/routes
- Debugging flows: using request logs + trace to root-cause timeouts and tokenization failures
- RBAC, KMS, VPC considerations on Dedicated/Private
- Benchmark and proof-of-concept scope

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for carving out time, uh, today. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Arjun here from Solutions.
[00:12] Arjun Patel: Hey, hi all. I'll primarily run through the console and the tracing bits, but please stop me with questions.
[00:20] Sara Gomez: Great, thanks. We're especially keen on how you surface errors and correlate them to customer requests. We get a lot of noisy failures in prod and need a better path to debug.
[00:31] Maya Chen: Totally, that's the goal. Quick qualification — Sara, Timothy, can you remind us what your current stack looks like and what you're calling into? Hosted third-party model endpoints or your own infra?
[00:43] Sara Gomez: We're running most inference through an in-house endpoint that proxies to several vendors; for now we're using OpenAI for few-shot and a private LLM for PII redaction. The proxy logs basic latency but no token-level traces.
[00:58] Timothy Lee: We care about latency percentiles — p50/p95/p99 — and also the source of errors: upstream timeouts vs model OOMs vs bad prompts causing stop sequences.
[01:12] Arjun Patel: Makes sense. I'll show how Redwood ties request logs to traces and where we add model-level metadata like KV-cache hits, quantization profile, and instance ID so you can see whether it's infra or model. Quick note: sometimes our transcriber picks up KV cache as 'KV cash' in the UI export — ignore that, it's the same thing.
[01:36] Maya Chen: Also, Nina, we flagged you'll likely have questions about SOC2, KMS, and network isolation — we prepared the compliance deck. We'll drop it after the call.
[01:47] Nina Park: Yep, thanks. Our security lead will want to see encryption at rest, KMS integration, and how audit logs look for admin actions.
[01:56] Arjun Patel: Absolutely. Okay jumping in — screen share — Console > Tracing.
[02:05] Arjun Patel: At the top you can see a request heatmap, default filter for the last 24 hours. The trace view gives you the full call graph: frontend proxy, routing service, instance, and model execution span. You can click a span to see logs and payload snippets.
[02:26] Sara Gomez: That span 'model.exec' — does that include token timings?
[02:31] Arjun Patel: Yes, we capture per-token timing buckets when enabled — default is coarse to save ingestion cost, but you can turn on detailed token timing for specific routes.
[02:44] Timothy Lee: How does that affect cost and retention? We're not keen on storing token-level data for 90 days.
[02:51] Arjun Patel: Good question. Token-level traces are configurable by route and sampled; you can keep detailed traces for a short retention window, say 7 days, and keep aggregated metrics long term. We'll share the retention options doc.
[03:05] Maya Chen: One thing to highlight — you can create alerts off the trace spans, not just the overall request latency. So if model.exec exceeds X ms we trigger a workflow.
[03:15] Sara Gomez: Nice. Walk us through an example error path, like a timeout vs invalid input.
[03:20] Arjun Patel: Sure. Here's a recent trace with a 504. You can see the trace ends at the model.exec span with status 'deadline_exceeded'. Click request logs tab — it shows the raw request that hit the proxy and the downstream response. We also correlate to the model version and node id, which helps isolate whether it's a hot node OOM.
[03:41] [03:42] Timothy Lee: Can we search logs by customer request ID? We wrap calls with our own request-id header.
[03:46] Arjun Patel: Yes — request logs allow arbitrary header search, we automatically index common headers like x-request-id. You can also save searches as saved-filters.
[03:56] Sara Gomez: There was a session where we saw partial responses; how would you trace that?
[04:01] Arjun Patel: Partial responses often show as early socket close or as the model returning a stop token. In the trace you'll see a short model.exec span and then a downstream disconnect. The request logs will contain the partial payload and we keep a snippet of the stream so you can see the last tokens.
[04:20] Maya Chen: We sometimes hear customers ask for an end-to-end trace that joins their app logs with Redwood traces. We provide a trace-id header so you can stitch with your observability stack (e.g., Datadog, Honeycomb).
[04:32] Timothy Lee: Great — we use Datadog. How much overhead is adding that trace-id?
[04:36] Arjun Patel: Minimal. It's just a header propagation, we do sampling server-side.
[04:40] Nina Park: On the security side, how is the request log access controlled? We need admin-level audit trail.
[04:46] Arjun Patel: RBAC supports route-level permissions. Audit logs capture who viewed what trace and when; those are exportable to S3 or your SIEM for long-term retention. For Dedicated/Private we can enable HSM-backed KMS integration.
[05:00] Sara Gomez: Can you demo filtering by model version? We run multiple versions during canary rollouts.
[05:06] Arjun Patel: Yep — filter dropdown includes model, model.version, region, instance, and custom tags you can add per request. Here's a canary trace where model.version=2.3-canary and you can see higher latency for p95.
[05:24] [05:30] Maya Chen: One thing about canaries — you can set automatic fallback policies in the routing layer if canary latency spikes above threshold.
[05:36] Timothy Lee: That's interesting. If we do Dedicated, will that routing fallback still apply?
[05:40] Arjun Patel: With Dedicated you can configure routing to prefer Dedicated pools and fall back to hosted variants in a different pool or region. There's a policy layer exposed in the Console.
[05:51] Sara Gomez: We often need to correlate user-level input (PII) with traces but we cannot keep PII in logs. How do you handle that?
[05:58] Arjun Patel: We support redaction at ingestion via regex or a pre-processing hook. For Private installs you can run the redaction step on-prem before sending traces.
[06:11] Nina Park: Good — and for KMS, is envelope encryption supported?
[06:15] Arjun Patel: Yes, envelope + customer-managed keys. For Dedicated you'll point to your KMS or HSM; for Hosted we integrate with AWS KMS/GCP KMS and support rotation policies.
[06:26] [06:28] Maya Chen: I also wanted to show the error analysis page. It aggregates error classes by route and model version. You can click into a spike and it pre-filters traces and logs for that window.
[06:39] Arjun Patel: Example — here you see a spike labeled 'inference_timeout' with a list of sample request logs. Clicking one opens the full trace with timings. You can export selected traces as a CSV or JSON for incident tickets.
[06:54] Timothy Lee: If we export to our ticketing system, can we include the raw payload? Some compliance teams won't allow it.
[07:00] Arjun Patel: You can toggle payload inclusion on export. By default we scrub PII and you can apply additional redaction rules.
[07:08] Sara Gomez: About long-running requests — do you persist partial traces if a client reconnects later? We have intermittent mobile connections.
[07:16] Arjun Patel: We store stream checkpoints and will stitch segments if the client provides the same request-id. Stitching is eventually consistent but usually sufficient for debugging.
[07:28] Maya Chen: I want to highlight the request logs tab — it has structured fields: request_headers, route, model.version, cost_estimate, and error_code. You can pivot on cost to find expensive outliers.
[07:42] [07:44] Timothy Lee: Cost estimates built into the trace are helpful. How accurate are they?
[07:48] Arjun Patel: They're based on per-token compute estimate and model profile; within a few percent for typical runs. For very spiky workloads we recommend running a short benchmark on Dedicated to calibrate.
[08:00] Sara Gomez: Can we schedule that benchmark as part of the POC?
[08:03] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll do that — see next steps.
[08:07] Arjun Patel: Back to debugging — here's a live example where a request fails with 'model.decoder_error' and we show stack traces from the runtime, node memory usage, and recent kernel logs if you have node-level access on Dedicated.
[08:24] Nina Park: Do you surface kernel-level logs for Hosted?
[08:28] Arjun Patel: For Hosted we surface runtime-level metrics and logs; for Dedicated we can enable node-level export to your logging endpoint.
[08:36] Sara Gomez: Do you have examples of rule-based automated remediations? Like auto-retry with backoff if it's a transient network blip?
[08:44] Arjun Patel: Yes, the reroute policy can auto-retry to a different pool or degrade model quality (switch to a smaller variant) automatically for some classes of error. You can see those in the rollout policy config.
[08:58] [09:00] Maya Chen: I'm going to show Request Logs search syntax quickly — you can search by header, by response status, or free text in payload snippet.
[09:10] Arjun Patel: Also worth showing is the saved-playbook feature — you can create a debugging playbook that runs a set of searches and collects outputs for an incident.
[09:20] Timothy Lee: That could map to our incident runbook. Nice.
[09:24] Sara Gomez: Switching gears — how do you handle model rollbacks? If a canary regresses, can we force traffic back to previous version automatically?
[09:31] Arjun Patel: Yes. The rollout UI supports immediate rollbacks, gradual traffic shifts, and auto-rollbacks based on metrics or quality regressions (integrated with Redwood Optimize to compare evals).
[09:45] Maya Chen: Quick question — are you planning any on-prem or VPC deployments? That affects the audit log and network diagram we send.
[09:52] Sara Gomez: Possibly. For PHI handling we'd prefer Dedicated in a VPC or Private on-prem for a subset of workloads.
[09:59] Nina Park: We need info on data residency and mutability — does Redwood allow customer-controlled purge?
[10:06] Arjun Patel: Customers can configure retention and purge on request logs/traces; on Dedicated/Private you have full control and we offer support to run deletion jobs.
[10:15] Maya Chen: I'm going to show an example incident timeline — here's an error spike at 02:12 UTC; using the timeline you can jump to traces and then open the raw request payload. The timeline also shows correlated infra events like node restarts.
[10:29] Sara Gomez: Nice, can we tag traces with our internal service names?
[10:33] Arjun Patel: Yep, custom tags are supported. We recommend propagating your service name header so the trace automatically gets the tag.
[10:40] [11:00] Timothy Lee: A quick question on log retention costs — what's the pricing model? Is log ingest charged separately?
[11:06] Maya Chen: Logs and traces are meterable; we have tiered pricing and can package longer retention in Enterprise add-on. We'll include pricing options in the follow-up.
[11:15] Nina Park: For SOC2 evidence, can we get a sample of the audit log export and the network diagram?
[11:21] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll send the SOC2 pack and a network diagram that shows Dedicated network flows.
[11:27] Sara Gomez: One more operational question — if we see a new error class, can we annotate it and ask Redwood support to triage?
[11:33] Arjun Patel: Yes, support tickets can reference trace IDs; our SEs can look up the trace, and for Dedicated we can run live debug sessions with node access if authorized.
[11:44] Maya Chen: I'm going to demo the request log export to S3 — here we set up an export job and you can choose partition by date, model, or route.
[11:55] Timothy Lee: Does export include encryption at rest on S3?
[11:59] Arjun Patel: We support SSE-KMS and will use your KMS key if provided.
[12:06] [12:20] Sara Gomez: About alerts — can we send alerts to PagerDuty with the trace URL?
[12:23] Arjun Patel: Absolutely, PagerDuty and Slack integrations included; the alert payload contains a direct link to the trace and a short excerpt of the logs.
[12:33] Maya Chen: We try to keep the demo practical — okay, switching to a debugging flow scenario: customer reports a class of tokenization errors for emojis.
[12:44] Arjun Patel: Here's the trace; the tokenizer span shows an unexpected token length and we surface the raw input snippet. The fix was to normalize input on the client side before sending. We annotated the playbook to include that normalization step.
[12:59] Sara Gomez: We've seen similar with non-utf8 inputs. Can Redwood auto-normalize?
[13:04] Arjun Patel: Not by default for Hosted, but you can add a pre-processor lambda in the client or use Private to run pre-processing on your side.
[13:12] Nina Park: Any concerns about shipping PII to Hosted for debug?
[13:16] Arjun Patel: For sensitive data we recommend redaction at ingestion or using Dedicated/Private deployments where data never leaves your VPC.
[13:26] [13:40] Timothy Lee: Let's talk SLA — Dedicated has a higher SLA?
[13:43] Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated comes with an SLA for uptime and latency targets, and committed capacity removes noisy neighbor concerns. We'll include SLA language in the contract appendix.
[13:58] Sara Gomez: If we need on-prem later, is migration path documented?
[14:02] Arjun Patel: We have migration guides — many customers start Hosted, move to Dedicated, then selectively move high-security workloads to Private.
[14:12] Maya Chen: Okay, demo wrap-up — going to summarize the key debugging features: trace-to-request linking, token timing, saved playbooks, redaction, RBAC/audit exports, and export to S3/SES.
[14:27] Timothy Lee: Quick clarification — you mentioned 'saved-playbook' export format; is that JSON?
[14:31] Arjun Patel: Yes JSON with trace IDs and saved query filters. Example repo link is in the deck: https://redwood.ai/console-playbooks (will share).
[14:45] Sara Gomez: One more operational ask — can you show how to set up auto-escalation when model quality drops?
[14:51] Arjun Patel: You can wire Redwood Optimize evals into the alerting pipeline; if eval scores drop below threshold, the policy can rollback a rollout or open a ticket.
[15:03] Maya Chen: Alright, let's move to questions and next steps.
[15:08] Sara Gomez: For the benchmark, how much setup work is required on our side?
[15:12] Arjun Patel: We'll provide a benchmark client and a small test harness. We need sample traffic and a model choice; we can run it against Hosted or Dedicated pools depending on what you want to validate.
[15:26] Timothy Lee: We'll likely test both — latency on Dedicated and cost differential with batching.
[15:32] Nina Park: For compliance, we need to know who will have visibility into traces in Redwood — is it per-user RBAC?
[15:38] Arjun Patel: Yes per-user RBAC and group-level roles. Audit logs capture reads and writes.
[15:44] Maya Chen: Cool. Any final questions?
[15:46] Sara Gomez: Not right now. Please send the SOC2 docs and pricing.
[15:50] Maya Chen: Will do.
[15:52] Arjun Patel: One more note — sometimes the console transcription shows 'KV cash' or 'canary canary' weird artifacts; apologies in advance for noisy exports.
[16:00] Sara Gomez: Haha noted.
[16:05] Maya Chen: Alright, recap of next steps — pricing, SOC2/network diagram, benchmark scheduling, trial access. We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the benchmark and set up a shared folder with the playbook repo.
[16:18] Timothy Lee: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[16:21] Nina Park: Thanks.
[16:23] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll send the notes.
[47:30] [call end — approximate 48m]

Notes on transcript quality: medium — occasional mis-transcriptions and filler words; speaker attributions are mostly correct but sometimes generic.

End of transcript.
